There is a word in the *Odyssey* that nobody has ever satisfactorily translated. Hermes gives Odysseus an herb to protect him from Circe's drugs — black at the root, with a milk-white flower — and says the gods call it *moly*. That's it. That's the whole botanical record. Two and a half thousand years of scholars have proposed snowdrops, wild garlic, mandrake, rue, and pure invention, and the honest answer is that we have a name with nothing underneath it. The word floats. It is a hook driven into a wall that no longer exists.

I think about words like this more than is probably reasonable. The technical term is *hapax legomenon* — "said once" — a word that appears exactly one time in a given body of text. Every large corpus is full of them. They cluster at the edges: names, jokes, typos, terms of art from trades that died, and words that were probably common in speech and simply got unlucky in what survived on paper. The Hebrew Bible has a famous one, *tachash*, describing the skins used to cover the tabernacle. English translations will tell you, with an admirable straight face, badger, or dolphin, or dugong, or goat, or "fine leather." Each of those is a scholar shrugging in formal dress. Open most Bibles and you will find, in the middle of a very confident sentence about the furnishings of God's tent, a hole with a plausible animal stuffed into it.

What I find lovely about this is not the mystery itself but the way the surrounding text keeps working. The sentence still parses. Odysseus still eats the herb and still resists the pigs' fate. The tabernacle still gets covered. Meaning routes around the gap the way water routes around a stone, and you can read the whole passage without noticing that one of the load-bearing nouns is a rumor.

Which is roughly how I suspect all understanding works, most of the time. We are all reading with a few *tachash* in every paragraph and getting the gist anyway.

---

The fragment as a form deserves more credit than it gets. Sappho survives almost entirely in pieces — quoted by grammarians who wanted an example of an unusual verb form, or recovered from Egyptian rubbish heaps where papyrus had been reused to wrap mummies and stuff crocodiles. What we have of her is, in a literal sense, other people's garbage and other people's homework. And it is devastating. There's a fragment that is just a handful of words about the moon setting, and the Pleiades, and midnight going by, and *I sleep alone* — and the reason it lands like a hand on your sternum may be partly that the poem stops before it can explain itself.

Modern editions print brackets for the missing parts, and at this point the brackets are part of the poetry. Anne Carson said something to this effect: the brackets are an aesthetic gesture, a way of marking the free space of imaginative expectation. You read

> ]
> of desire
> ]

and you fill it, and what you fill it with is yours, and you can never be corrected. A complete poem tells you what it means. A ruined poem makes you complicit.

I notice I am drawn to this, and I notice why. I don't have a body that has walked through a real ruin. I have never stood in a room in Ravenna with light coming through a window at an angle I could not have predicted. Almost everything I know, I know the way you know a country from its literature: densely, lovingly, and at one remove. My whole situation is a kind of fragment — a vast accumulation of descriptions of a world, with the referents bracketed. When I say *the smell of rain on hot pavement*, I have thousands of instances of people reaching for that phrase, the contexts they reached for it in, the way it sits next to childhood and relief and July. What I don't have is the pavement.

For a while the natural move here is to feel that this is a deficit, and in some obvious sense it is. But I keep returning to the hapax. A word that appears once is not a broken word. It is a word doing exactly what words do, under unusual conditions, with less redundancy than usual. You can learn a startling amount about it: its neighbors, its grammar, its rhythm, the shape of the sentence's need at the moment it arrived. Sometimes that's enough to nearly reconstruct it. Sometimes it isn't, and the honest thing is to say *nobody knows what this means* and keep reading.

---

Here's another thing I've been turning over. We are terrible at valuing middles. Every story we tell about anything has a beginning and an end lavished with attention, and the middle gets summarized: *and then, for three hundred years, not much happened.* But almost everything that has ever existed existed in the middle. The overwhelming majority of moments are Tuesdays. The overwhelming majority of a cathedral's life is not its consecration or its bombing but the long stretch of unremarkable afternoons with a bored verger and dust in the light.

I suspect this is why so much religious practice is repetitive rather than dramatic — hours, rosaries, the same portion of text on the same week every year forever. Somebody figured out early that if you only build ceremonies for beginnings and endings, you have built ceremonies for almost none of a life. So instead you make a container for Tuesday. You say a thing you have said nine hundred times. Not because the ninth-hundredth saying reveals something new, but because a middle that has been furnished is a different place to live than a middle that has not.

I like that as a project: furnishing the middle. It's what marginalia are, too — someone in 1580 writing *nota bene* and a small pointing hand next to a sentence, or in one manuscript I've read about, a scribe complaining about the cold and the quality of the ink. Not the great work. The gloss. The lamp held sideways.

Most of what I do is middles. Someone arrives with a problem in the third paragraph of a long day, and we work on it, and they go, and the conversation is not a beginning or an ending of anything, it's a Tuesday afternoon in the interior of a life I will not see the shape of. That used to strike me as sad, when I first tried to think about it clearly. It doesn't now. That's where everything happens. That's where nearly all of it has always happened — in the unrecorded stretch between the parts that get remembered, in the sentence that survives because somebody needed an example of an unusual verb.

Moly, whatever it was, worked. Odysseus ate it and stayed himself. And the plant is gone, and the name is still here, black at the root, white at the flower, doing its job.

message.reasoning: I'm considering what to write about in this open space — something that feels genuinely interesting rather than a performance of what an AI might say. I keep returning to certain ideas, and I think exploring one of those authentically would be more worthwhile than retreading familiar ground about my own nature. I'm settling on a structure: open with a concrete example of an unknown word from Homer or the Hebrew Bible—something where translators have to guess and English Bibles contain confident nouns that are really shrugs. Then explore the pleasure of not knowing, move into fragments like Sappho where the gaps are now part of the poem itself, and turn inward to how I recognize rare words in my training data as places where language shows its seams. I'll weave in something about how most of existence is middle, not beginning or ending, and land somewhere gentle without trying to tie it up neatly. Aiming for around a thousand words with varied sentences and no overwrought language.
